Resolution is sound and refutation-complete. Horn clauses (at most one positive literal) allow fast forward chaining (data-driven) and backward chaining (goal-driven) with modus ponens.
items.used_for: Automated theorem provers (Vampire, E), Prolog's SLD resolution, clause learning in CDCL SAT solvers, expert-system inference engines, Datalog. Book: Ch 54 (Resolution rule definition; Forward and backward chaining).

items.name: First-order logic: quantifiers, unification and generalized modus ponens
items.formula: ∀x P(x) is true iff P holds for every object; ∃x P(x) iff for at least one; ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x); UNIFY(p, q) = θ such that SUBST(θ, p) = SUBST(θ, q); generalized modus ponens: from p1', ..., pn' and (p1 ∧ ... ∧ pn ⇒ q) infer SUBST(θ, q), where SUBST(θ, pi') = SUBST(θ, pi) for every i
items.meaning: x is a variable; P a predicate (a property or relation); θ a substitution (variable bindings such as {x/Maria}); SUBST applies it. Example: 'every person who owns a car needs insurance' and 'Maria owns a car' unify to give 'Maria needs insurance'.
items.used_for: Prolog, knowledge representation and ontologies (description logics, OWL), knowledge-graph rule engines, interactive theorem proving. Book: Ch 54 (First-order logic).

items.name: STRIPS/PDDL action model for classical planning
items.formula: action a is applicable in state s iff PRECOND(a) ⊆ s; RESULT(s, a) = (s − DEL(a)) ∪ ADD(a); a plan is an action sequence leading from the initial state to a state that satisfies the goal
items.meaning: A state is the set of facts currently true; PRECOND the facts the action needs; ADD the facts it makes true; DEL the facts it makes false; ⊆ 'is contained in', − set difference, ∪ union. Planner heuristics come from relaxations that ignore delete lists (h_max, h_add, h_FF) and from planning graphs.
items.used_for: Shakey (1972), PDDL planners (Fast Downward, LAMA), space-mission and logistics planning, systems that have an LLM translate goals into PDDL for a classical planner. Book: Ch 48 (Planning with actions: from Shakey to PDDL).

items.name: Bayesian network joint factorization
items.formula: P(x_1, ..., x_n) = product over i of P(x_i | parents(X_i)); numbers needed = sum over i of (k_i − 1) × (product of its parents' sizes), versus (product of all k_i) − 1 for the full joint table
items.meaning: parents(X_i) are X_i's direct causes in a directed acyclic graph; each node carries a conditional probability table; k_i is the number of values X_i can take. The assumption: given its parents, a node is independent of its non-descendants. Book example: rain, sprinkler, wet grass need 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 numbers instead of 2^3 − 1 = 7; the saving grows exponentially with size. Naive Bayes is a special case (in the classical-ML section).
items.used_for: Medical diagnosis (Pathfinder), troubleshooting wizards, risk and reliability models, causal modeling. Book: Ch 54 (A Bayesian network, worked by hand).

items.name: Markov random fields, factor graphs and conditional random fields
items.formula: P(x) = (1 ÷ Z) × product over cliques c of ψ_c(x_c), with Z = sum over all x of product over c of ψ_c(x_c); CRF: P(y | x) = (1 ÷ Z(x)) × exp(sum over k of w_k × f_k(y, x))
items.meaning: ψ_c is a non-negative potential (compatibility score) over the variables x_c in clique c; Z the partition function; for a CRF, f_k are feature functions of labels y and input x with weights w_k. The undirected counterpart of a Bayesian network, and an energy-based model with E = −sum of ln ψ_c.
items.used_for: Image-segmentation smoothing (DeepLab's CRF post-processing, 2015-2017), sequence labeling (CRF taggers for named entities), factor-graph SLAM and sensor fusion (GTSAM), Ising-type models. Book: Ch 54 (Probabilistic graphical models: Markov random fields).

items.name: Inference by enumeration (normalization constant α)
items.formula: P(X | e) = α × P(X, e) = α × sum over y of P(X, e, y), with α = 1 ÷ P(e)
items.meaning: X is the query variable; e the observed evidence; y ranges over every combination of the hidden variables, which are 'summed out'; each P(X, e, y) is computed with the network's factorization; α rescales the answers to add to 1. 'Explaining away' falls out automatically. Exact inference is NP-hard in general (Cooper 1990).
items.used_for: Exact queries on small Bayesian networks; the definition every faster algorithm must match. Book: Ch 54 (A Bayesian network, worked by hand: explaining away).

items.name: Variable elimination and belief propagation
items.formula: factor product f(X, Y, Z) = f_1(X, Y) × f_2(Y, Z) (entry by entry); summing out f'(X, Z) = sum over y of f(X, y, Z); P(X | e) = α × (sum over the hidden variables, one at a time, of the product of factors); sum-product message on a tree m_(i→j)(x_j) = sum over x_i of ψ(x_i, x_j) × product over k ≠ j of m_(k→i)(x_i)
items.meaning: A factor is a table over a few variables; pushing each sum inside the product avoids recomputing shared pieces. Cost is exponential only in the largest intermediate factor (governed by the graph's treewidth). Belief propagation passes these partial sums as messages between neighbors; the HMM forward algorithm is a special case.
items.used_for: Exact Bayesian-network engines and the junction-tree algorithm; belief-propagation decoding of LDPC error-correcting codes (Wi-Fi, 5G). Book: only here.

items.name: Noisy-OR conditional distribution
items.formula: P(no effect | the set T of causes that are present) = product over j in T of q_j; P(effect | T) = 1 − product over j in T of q_j (with a leak cause, also multiply by q_0)
items.meaning: q_j is the probability that cause j, acting alone, fails to produce the effect; k causes need only k numbers instead of a 2^k-row table; the leak q_0 covers causes not in the model.
items.used_for: Large diagnostic networks (the QMR-DT medical network), fault diagnosis. Book: only here.

items.name: Approximate inference by sampling: likelihood weighting, Gibbs sampling and Metropolis–Hastings
items.formula: likelihood weighting: sample the non-evidence variables in parent-first order and weight each sample w = product over evidence variables E_i of P(e_i | parents(E_i)); estimate P(x | e) ≈ (sum of w over samples with X = x) ÷ (sum of all w); Gibbs: resample X_i from P(X_i | mb(X_i)) = α × P(x_i | parents(X_i)) × product over children Y_j of P(y_j | parents(Y_j)); Metropolis–Hastings: accept a proposal x' with probability min(1, (p(x') × q(x | x')) ÷ (p(x) × q(x' | x)))
items.meaning: mb(X_i) is X_i's Markov blanket (parents, children and the children's other parents); q a proposal distribution; Gibbs and Metropolis–Hastings are Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods whose long-run samples follow the posterior. Rejection sampling is the naive alternative that discards samples disagreeing with the evidence.
items.used_for: Probabilistic programming (Stan, PyMC), Bayesian statistics, inference in large Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, sampling energy-based models. Book: only here.

items.name: Causal effect by back-door adjustment (the do-operator)
items.formula: P(y | do(x)) = sum over z of P(y | x, z) × P(z), where Z blocks every back-door path from X to Y
items.meaning: do(x) means X is set by intervention rather than observed; Z is a set of variables (confounders) that, once conditioned on, leaves no non-causal path between X and Y. Differs from the observational P(y | x) whenever confounders exist.
items.used_for: Causal Bayesian networks (AIMA 4th edition, Pearl), uplift and policy evaluation in advertising and medicine, debiasing observational data. Book: only here.

items.name: Hidden Markov model joint probability
items.formula: P(x_0, ..., x_T, e_1, ..., e_T) = P(x_0) × product over t = 1..T of P(x_t | x_(t−1)) × P(e_t | x_t); transition matrix A_ij = P(x_t = j | x_(t−1) = i); emission B_j(e) = P(e | x_t = j)
items.meaning: x_t is the hidden state at time t (e.g., which phoneme, or whether it is raining); e_t the observation (evidence); the next state depends only on the current one (first-order Markov assumption) and each observation only on the current state (sensor Markov assumption). Kalman filters (Gaussian states) and particle filters share this structure (a dynamic Bayesian network).
items.used_for: Speech recognition from the 1980s to the early 2010s, part-of-speech tagging, gene finding and profile HMMs in bioinformatics, gesture recognition. Book: Ch 54 (filters and the umbrella example; HMM definition); Ch 46.

items.name: Bayes filter and the HMM forward algorithm (filtering), with the POMDP belief update
items.formula: predict: P(x_(t+1) | e_(1:t)) = sum over x_t of P(x_(t+1) | x_t) × P(x_t | e_(1:t)); update: P(x_(t+1) | e_(1:t+1)) = η × P(e_(t+1) | x_(t+1)) × P(x_(t+1) | e_(1:t)); unnormalized forward variable α_t(j) = B_j(e_t) × sum over i of α_(t−1)(i) × A_ij, with P(e_(1:T)) = sum over j of α_T(j); POMDP: b'(s') = η × P(o | s') × sum over s of P(s' | s, a) × b(s)
items.meaning: The belief is a probability distribution over the hidden state; η a normalizing constant (written α in AIMA, not to be confused with the forward variable α_t); predict with the motion (transition) model, then correct with the sensor model. A POMDP planner applies the same update after choosing action a and observing o. Kalman and particle filters are this recursion for Gaussian and sampled beliefs. Cost per step O(S^2) for S states.
items.used_for: Robot localization and tracking, HMM speech decoding, belief tracking in POMDP planners and dialogue systems. Book: Ch 54 (filters that track a hidden state over time; umbrella example).

items.name: Forward–backward smoothing
items.formula: backward variable β_t(i) = sum over j of A_ij × B_j(e_(t+1)) × β_(t+1)(j), with β_T(i) = 1; smoothed γ_t(i) = P(x_t = i | e_(1:T)) = α_t(i) × β_t(i) ÷ P(e_(1:T))
items.meaning: β_t(i) is the probability of all later evidence given state i at time t; γ_t combines past and future evidence ('was it really raining on Monday?'). Cost O(T × S^2).
items.used_for: Offline tracking and annotation, Baum–Welch training, the same dynamic program as the CTC loss, gene annotation. Book: Ch 54 (Smoothing).

items.name: Viterbi algorithm (most likely hidden-state sequence)
items.formula: δ_t(j) = B_j(e_t) × max over i of (δ_(t−1)(i) × A_ij); backpointer ψ_t(j) = argmax over i of (δ_(t−1)(i) × A_ij); end at argmax over j of δ_T(j) and follow the backpointers; log form ln δ_t(j) = ln B_j(e_t) + max over i of (ln δ_(t−1)(i) + ln A_ij)
items.meaning: δ_t(j) is the probability of the single best path that ends in state j at time t; ψ stores where that path came from; it is the forward algorithm with the sum replaced by a max. Logs prevent numerical underflow. Cost O(T × S^2).
items.used_for: HMM speech recognizers, decoding convolutional error-correcting codes in phones and Wi-Fi, part-of-speech tagging, CRF decoding, gene finding. Book: Ch 54 (Viterbi algorithm).

items.name: Baum–Welch algorithm (EM for hidden Markov models)
items.formula: ξ_t(i, j) = α_t(i) × A_ij × B_j(e_(t+1)) × β_(t+1)(j) ÷ P(e_(1:T)); A_ij ← (sum over t of ξ_t(i, j)) ÷ (sum over t of γ_t(i)); B_j(k) ← (sum over t with e_t = k of γ_t(j)) ÷ (sum over t of γ_t(j))
items.meaning: ξ_t(i, j) is the expected probability of moving from state i to state j at time t; γ the smoothed state probabilities; re-estimate and repeat. Each round never lowers the likelihood (it is expectation–maximization, whose general form is in the classical-ML section).
items.used_for: Training HMM speech recognizers before 2012; profile HMMs in bioinformatics (HMMER). Book: only here.

items.name: Kalman filter predict step
items.meaning: x̂ is the state estimate (e.g., position and velocity); F the state-transition (motion) matrix; u_t a control input with matrix B; P the covariance (uncertainty) of the estimate; Q the process-noise covariance; the ⁻ mark means 'before this step's measurement'. Uncertainty grows at every prediction. 1D version: μ⁻ = μ + motion, P⁻ = P + Q.
items.used_for: GPS and inertial navigation, the Apollo guidance computer, object tracking in self-driving perception, robot localization and EKF-SLAM, multi-object trackers in computer vision (SORT, ByteTrack). Book: Ch 54 (Kalman filter definition); Ch 50 (Localization; Prediction).

items.name: Kalman filter update step (Kalman gain)
items.meaning: z_t is the measurement; H maps a state to the reading it should produce; R the sensor-noise covariance; K the Kalman gain (0 = ignore the sensor, 1 = trust it fully); z − H × x̂⁻ the innovation (surprise). Optimal for linear systems with Gaussian noise. The extended Kalman filter linearizes nonlinear models with Jacobians; the unscented Kalman filter propagates a few 'sigma points'.
items.used_for: Same systems as the predict step. Book: Ch 54 (Kalman filter: predict-and-correct arithmetic).

items.name: Particle filter (sequential importance resampling)
items.formula: move each particle x_t^(i) ~ P(x_t | x_(t−1)^(i), u_t); weight w^(i) ∝ P(z_t | x_t^(i)); normalize w^(i) ← w^(i) ÷ sum over j of w^(j); effective sample size N_eff = 1 ÷ sum over i of (w^(i))^2; resample N particles with probabilities w^(i) (typically when N_eff falls below N ÷ 2)
items.meaning: i indexes the N particles (guesses of the state); the motion model moves them; the sensor model scores them against measurement z_t; resampling copies good particles and drops poor ones. Handles non-Gaussian, many-peaked beliefs that a Kalman filter cannot.
items.used_for: Monte Carlo localization in mobile robots and robot vacuums, FastSLAM, visual tracking. Book: Ch 54 (Particle filter definition).

items.name: Occupancy-grid log-odds update
items.formula: l_(t, i) = l_(t−1, i) + ln(p(m_i | z_t, x_t) ÷ (1 − p(m_i | z_t, x_t))) − l_0; P(cell i occupied) = 1 − 1 ÷ (1 + exp(l_(t, i)))
items.meaning: l is the log-odds that cell i is occupied; p(m_i | z_t, x_t) the inverse sensor model (probability the cell is occupied given this reading z_t and robot pose x_t); l_0 the prior log-odds (0 for a 50% prior). Adding log-odds equals multiplying odds, which is Bayes' rule for a yes/no variable.
items.used_for: Robot vacuums and warehouse robots, lidar mapping and SLAM, self-driving occupancy grids (increasingly predicted directly by networks). Book: Ch 50 (Occupancy grid definition).

items.name: Forward kinematics and transform chains
items.formula: two-link planar arm: x = l_1 × cos(θ_1) + l_2 × cos(θ_1 + θ_2), y = l_1 × sin(θ_1) + l_2 × sin(θ_1 + θ_2); general chain T_(base→hand) = T_1(θ_1) × T_2(θ_2) × ... × T_n(θ_n) (4 × 4 homogeneous transforms); numerical inverse kinematics Δθ = J^+ × Δx
items.meaning: l_1 and l_2 are link lengths; θ_1 and θ_2 joint angles; each T_i is joint i's 'rotate, then shift' transform; J the Jacobian of hand position with respect to joint angles and J^+ its pseudo-inverse; Δx a small desired hand motion. Inverse kinematics may have many solutions or none.
items.used_for: Robot arms and humanoids, animation rigs; robot foundation models that output hand poses rely on IK to turn them into joint commands. Book: Ch 49 (From 'go there' to motor commands: Forward and inverse kinematics; Coordinate frame).

items.name: PID controller
items.formula: u(t) = K_p × e(t) + K_i × (integral from 0 to t of e(τ) dτ) + K_d × de(t) ÷ dt, with e = target − measured; discrete form u_k = K_p × e_k + K_i × (sum over j ≤ k of e_j × Δt) + K_d × (e_k − e_(k−1)) ÷ Δt
items.meaning: u is the control output (e.g., motor torque); e the error; K_p, K_i and K_d the proportional, integral and derivative gains; Δt the control period. The integral term removes steady offsets (an arm sagging under gravity); the derivative term brakes before overshoot.
items.used_for: Low-level joint control underneath learned robot policies, drones, cruise control, industrial process control. Book: Ch 49 (Holding steady: PID controller worked example).

items.name: Model predictive control objective
items.formula: at each control step solve min over u_0, ..., u_(H−1) of sum over k = 0..H−1 of (||x_k − x_ref,k||_Q^2 + ||u_k||_R^2) subject to x_(k+1) = f(x_k, u_k) and limits on x and u; apply only u_0, measure, and solve again
items.meaning: H is the planning horizon; f the dynamics model (hand-derived or learned); x_ref the desired trajectory; ||v||_Q^2 = v^T × Q × v a weighted squared error, with Q and R trading tracking accuracy against control effort. Sampling-based variants (MPPI, the cross-entropy method) work with learned world models.
items.used_for: Legged robots, self-driving planning and control, process control; planning in learned world models: V-JEPA 2-AC (2025) picks robot actions with the cross-entropy method by minimizing the L1 distance between predicted and goal embeddings. Book: Ch 49 (Model predictive control definition).

items.name: RRT extension step (sampling-based motion planning)
items.formula: sample x_rand; x_near = argmin over tree nodes x of ||x − x_rand||; x_new = x_near + η × (x_rand − x_near) ÷ ||x_rand − x_near||; add x_new if the segment from x_near is collision-free; RRT* rewires neighbors within radius r ∝ (ln(n) ÷ n)^(1/d)
items.meaning: x are points in configuration space (joint angles or vehicle poses); η the step size; n the number of nodes in the tree; d the dimension of the space. RRT quickly explores high-dimensional spaces; RRT* converges to the shortest path. The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) is the multi-query cousin.
items.used_for: Robot-arm motion planning (MoveIt and OMPL), automated parking, drones. Book: Ch 49 (RRT definition; Configuration space).

items.name: Expected utility and the maximum-expected-utility principle
items.formula: EU(a) = sum over outcomes s' of P(s' | a) × U(s'); choose a* = argmax over a of EU(a)
items.meaning: a is an action; s' a possible outcome; P(s' | a) its probability if a is taken; U(s') its utility (how desirable it is). AIMA defines a rational agent as one that maximizes expected utility. Decision networks add decision and utility nodes to a Bayesian network to compute it.
items.used_for: Decision-theoretic agents, medical decision support, robot task selection; it is the expected-reward objective that reinforcement learning optimizes. Book: Ch 48 (Deciding when you are not sure: expected utility).

items.name: Value of perfect information (VPI)
items.formula: VPI(E) = (sum over values e of P(E = e) × max over a of EU(a | E = e)) − max over a of EU(a); VPI ≥ 0; gather the information only if VPI exceeds its cost
items.meaning: E is an unknown variable you could observe (a test, a sensor reading, a clarifying question); the formula compares the average value of deciding after seeing E with the value of deciding now. Information that cannot change the decision is worth nothing.
items.used_for: Choosing medical tests, sensor placement, active learning, agents deciding whether to ask a clarifying question or call a tool before acting. Book: Ch 48 (value of information).

items.name: Utility of money, risk attitude and multiattribute utility
items.formula: risk aversion: U(E[X]) > E[U(X)] for a concave U (e.g., U(w) = ln(w)); certainty equivalent CE solves U(CE) = E[U(X)]; risk premium = E[X] − CE; additive multiattribute utility U(x_1, ..., x_n) = sum over i of w_i × u_i(x_i)
items.meaning: X is an uncertain amount of money; w wealth; a concave utility prefers a sure thing to a gamble with the same average; w_i are attribute weights and u_i single-attribute utilities (the additive form is valid when the attributes are mutually preferentially independent).
items.used_for: Decision support, preference elicitation, multi-objective agent and reward design. Book: only here (Ch 48 introduces expected utility).

items.name: Value iteration and policy iteration (planning with a known MDP model)
items.formula: value iteration: U_(i+1)(s) = max over a of sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) × (R(s, a, s') + γ × U_i(s')); stop when the largest change is below ε × (1 − γ) ÷ γ; policy iteration: evaluate U^π(s) = sum over s' of P(s' | s, π(s)) × (R(s, π(s), s') + γ × U^π(s')), then improve π(s) ← argmax over a of sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) × (R(s, a, s') + γ × U^π(s')), until π stops changing
items.meaning: s and s' are states; a an action; P the known transition model; R the reward; γ the discount factor between 0 and 1; U the utility (value) of each state; π a policy; ε the error tolerance. Its fixed point is the Bellman optimality equation (given in the reinforcement-learning section); here the model is known, so this is planning, not learning from trial and error.
items.used_for: Grid-world and robot-navigation planning, inventory and maintenance planning, point-based POMDP solvers, planning steps inside model-based RL. Book: Ch 48 (Markov decision processes: the formal frame; Value iteration definition).

items.name: Fuzzy membership, fuzzy operators and defuzzification
items.formula: membership μ_A(x) between 0 and 1, e.g. a ramp μ_warm(x) = max(0, min(1, (x − a) ÷ (b − a))); μ_(A AND B) = min(μ_A, μ_B); μ_(A OR B) = max(μ_A, μ_B); μ_(NOT A) = 1 − μ_A; weighted-average (centroid-style) defuzzification output = (sum over rules r of μ_r × y_r) ÷ (sum over rules r of μ_r)
items.meaning: μ_A(x) is the degree to which x belongs to the vague category A; a and b are where the ramp starts and ends; μ_r a rule's firing strength and y_r its output value (e.g., fan speed). Degrees of truth are not probabilities. Book worked example: at 27 °C, warm = 0.2 and hot = 0.5 give (8 + 50) ÷ 0.7 ≈ 83% fan speed.
